title: Developing indicators to support investment opportunities in nature‐positive outcomes on solar farms
content:
We present 13 metrics that could be used to assess different aspects of natural capital and ecosystem services for internal and external reporting and disclosures related to nature-positive investments in solar farms. We identified four hierarchical levels of indicator use by stakeholders: site-level management, core industry including internal reporting, ESG reporting and financial disclosures, and investment and green finance.


Abstract

Solar farms can deliver a suite of biodiversity and ecosystem co-benefits (e.g. soil carbon storage) in addition to low carbon electricity if suitably designed, sited and managed. Indicators and metrics of biodiversity and ecosystem services are essential for assessing nature-positive outcomes on solar farms, and are increasingly required for Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) reporting, nature-related financial disclosures and monitoring nature-positive investments. However, the appropriate indicators and metrics for stakeholders from different parts of the solar farm value chain are not well resolved. We used literature to assemble a longlist of indicators and metrics relating to biodiversity and ecosystem services on solar farms. We also carried out interviews and workshops with stakeholders involved in solar farm investment, monitoring, operations and management in the UK. We then developed ‘good indicator’ criteria (including credibility, meaningfulness, feasibility and communicability/acceptability to stakeholders), which we used to refine the longlist into a set of metrics suitable for use within nature-related financial disclosure frameworks. Our initial longlist of indicators comprised 97 potential metrics across 19 indicator categories. This was subsequently refined to a shortlist of 20 metrics and then a final list of 13 metrics relating to aspects of ecosystem extent, connectivity, condition, and ecosystem services. We identified four hierarchical levels of indicator use by stakeholders: site-level management, core industry including internal reporting, ESG reporting and financial disclosures, and investment and green finance. Land managers value practical and feasible indicators and metrics for use at the solar farm scale, whereas financial stakeholders require scalable, comparable indicators that map onto wider ESG reporting and disclosure frameworks to ensure compliance. Challenges when identifying appropriate indicators and metrics for monitoring nature-positive investments in solar farms include spatial and temporal variability, scalability, data comparison and the potential for trade-offs between ecosystem services. Practical implication. We present 13 metrics that could be used to assess different aspects of natural capital and ecosystem services for internal and external reporting and disclosures related to nature-positive investments in solar farms. We suggest potential solutions to the challenges associated with nature-related metrics and stakeholder needs.
